S01.title: A Kind Act
S01.passage:
It was a warm Friday morning. Eight-year-old Benny was walking to school with his bag on his back. Just as he turned the corner, he saw an elderly woman standing still on the pavement. She was holding a heavy bag of groceries and looking at the busy road with a worried face.

Benny stopped. He looked at his watch — he had just enough time before school started. He walked up to her and said politely, 'Excuse me, may I help you cross the road?'

The woman looked at him in surprise. Then she smiled and said, 'Oh, how kind! Yes, please.'

Benny waited for the green man to appear. He took the woman's bag and held her hand gently as they crossed the road together. On the other side, the woman thanked him again and again.

Benny arrived at school just as the bell rang. His teacher, Mr Aziz, noticed that he was slightly out of breath. When Benny explained what had happened, Mr Aziz nodded and said, 'You made a good choice this morning, Benny. Being kind is never a waste of time.'

S02.title: The Lost Cat
S02.passage:
Nine-year-old Nina had a tabby cat named Biscuit. One Thursday afternoon, she came home from school and found the front door slightly open. She looked everywhere for Biscuit but could not find him. Nina felt sick with worry.

She told her mother, who suggested they make some posters. Together, they printed twelve posters with Biscuit's photo and their phone number on them. Nina and her father walked around the neighbourhood and stuck the posters on lamp posts and notice boards.

The next morning, a neighbour from the next block called. She saw Biscuit sitting under her car. Nina ran all the way to the neighbour's house. There was Biscuit, thin and hungry but otherwise unhurt.

Nina's eyes filled with tears as she carried him home. She promised herself she would always check the front door carefully before leaving the house.

S03.title: The Surprise Party
S03.passage:
Eight-year-old Nora planned a surprise birthday party for her father for two weeks. She made a list of things to do and checked off each item carefully. She baked a chocolate cake with help from her grandmother. She drew a large banner that said 'Happy Birthday, Dad!' and hung it across the living room doorway.

On the morning of the party, Nora and her mother went to the market to buy fresh flowers and fruit. Nora chose yellow sunflowers because they were her father's favourite. When they came home, her brother was blowing up balloons in the kitchen.

That evening, their neighbours and relatives arrived quietly. Everyone hid behind the sofa and the curtains. When Dad walked in from work and turned on the lights, everyone jumped out and shouted, 'Surprise!'

Dad stood still for a moment, his mouth open in shock. Then his eyes grew watery, and he hugged Nora tightly. 'I had no idea,' he whispered. 'This is the best gift I have ever received.'

S04.title: The Flooded Market
S04.passage:
On a stormy Wednesday, heavy rain flooded the market near Greenwood Estate. Water rose quickly to ankle level, and some stalls had to close. Mrs Chen, who ran a fruit stall, was packing up her unsold mangoes in a hurry.

Suddenly, she heard a splash behind her. She turned around and saw an elderly man called Mr Siva sitting on the wet ground. He had slipped on the flooded floor. His groceries were scattered everywhere.

Mrs Chen called for help loudly. Three young men who were nearby rushed over. Two of them helped Mr Siva to his feet while the third picked up his groceries. They found a dry spot under a stall roof and sat Mr Siva down there.

Mr Siva rubbed his knee and said he was all right. One of the young men offered to take him home in a taxi. At first, Mr Siva said it was not necessary. But they insisted, and he finally agreed.

The next day, Mr Siva returned to the market. He went to the fruit stall and left a bag of oranges for Mrs Chen with a note that said: 'Thank you for shouting for help. You saved me from sitting in the rain alone.'

S05.title: The Fishball Noodle Uncle
S05.passage:
Every morning, Mr Lim arrived at his stall at five o'clock, long before the rest of the hawker centre opened. He boiled the fishball soup for at least two hours to get the right taste. Mr Lim sold fishball noodles at Tampines Food Centre for over twenty years.

One rainy Tuesday, a young boy came to the stall alone. He looked at the menu and counted his coins carefully. 'Uncle,' he said quietly, 'I only have one dollar and fifty cents. Is that enough for a small bowl?'

Mr Lim looked at the boy. He knew the price was two dollars. But the boy's wet uniform and tired eyes told him the boy had come a long way in the rain. 'Of course,' said Mr Lim with a smile. 'One dollar fifty is enough today.'

He served the boy a full bowl — not a small one. He even added extra fishballs. The boy ate every bit of it and looked up at Mr Lim with bright eyes. 'Thank you, Uncle. This is the best I have ever eaten.'

Mr Lim waved his hand. 'Come back any time,' he said. And he meant it.

S06.title: The Day the River Flooded
S06.passage:
It rained for three days without stopping. The river near Kai's village began to rise higher and higher. On the third morning, Kai woke up to find that water had seeped under the front door of their house.

'We have to leave now,' said Grandfather. He was a farmer who lived in the village all his life and saw floods before. 'Take only what you need,' he told the family.

Kai quickly grabbed his schoolbag and packed it with his books, a change of clothes and his grandmother's old photo album. His little sister Maya carried her favourite toy rabbit. Mother packed some food and medicine.

The family waded through ankle-deep water to reach higher ground. Neighbours helped each other along the way. At the community hall, volunteers were handing out blankets and hot drinks.

Three days later, the rain stopped and the water went down. When the family returned home, they found mud on the floors and some furniture damaged. But Grandfather looked around and smiled. 'We are safe. We can clean and fix the rest,' he said.

S07.title: The Last Lap
S07.passage:
It was the final race of the year — the 1500-metre run. Twelve-year-old Priya stood at the starting line, her heart beating fast. She had trained for months for this moment.

The race began. For the first two laps, Priya stayed in third place, pacing herself carefully. Her coach, Mr Rajan, had always told her: 'Save your energy for the last lap.'

On the third lap, the girl in first place stumbled and fell. She got up quickly, but she lost precious time. Priya pushed forward and moved into second place.

With one lap to go, Priya's legs felt heavy. She thought about giving up. But then she heard the crowd cheering and she remembered why she started running — not to win, but to prove to herself that she could finish.

She crossed the finish line in second place. As she caught her breath, she felt a deep sense of pride. Mr Rajan ran over and shook her hand. 'That,' he said, 'was your best race ever.'

S09.title: The Old Tree
S09.passage:
At the centre of Birchwood Primary School stood a magnificent old raintree. Its wide branches spread across the entire field, giving shade to students during recess. According to the school's history book, the tree was planted by the school's founder over eighty years ago.

One morning, the principal announced that the raintree had to be cut down because its roots were cracking the floor of the school hall. Many students were upset. A group of Primary 5 students decided to do something about it.

They started a petition and collected over three hundred signatures from students, teachers and parents. They also researched ways to save old trees without cutting them down. One student found that roots could be guided away from buildings using special underground barriers.

The principal read the petition carefully. Impressed by the students' effort and research, she agreed to bring in a tree expert before making the final decision.

The expert visited and suggested installing root barriers underground to guide the roots away from the hall. It would cost more, but the tree could be saved.

A month later, the work was done. The old raintree still stood, and students still gathered under its shade during recess, just as they always did.

S10.title: The Secret Recipe
S10.passage:
Every Chinese New Year, Great-Aunt Lian made her famous pineapple tarts. People said they were the best in the whole neighbourhood. Families would come from nearby streets just to get a small tin of them.

This year, Great-Aunt Lian was eighty years old. Her hands shook a little as she rolled the pastry, but her eyes were sharp and her instructions were clear. Twelve-year-old Nadia sat beside her, watching every movement carefully.

'The secret,' said Great-Aunt Lian, 'is not the recipe. It is the patience.' She showed Nadia how to press each small circle of pastry gently, how to place just the right amount of filling in the centre, and how to seal the edges without cracking them.

By the afternoon, they made three hundred tarts. Nadia's back ached and her fingers were sticky with sugar, but she did not complain. She was too busy learning.

'You have good hands,' said Great-Aunt Lian at the end of the day. 'Next year, you can make them yourself.'

Nadia felt a warmth spread through her chest. She realised that Great-Aunt Lian was not just teaching her to bake. She was passing down something that words alone could not explain.

On the train, Zara found her seat and placed her backpack on the overhead rack. A kind elderly man in the next seat asked her where she was going. When she told him, he smiled. 'Singapore! I used to live there thirty years ago,' he said.

They talked all the way to Johor Bahru. The man told Zara about the Singapore he remembered — the food, the people and the kampung house he grew up in. Zara listened with great interest.

When the train pulled into Woodlands Checkpoint, Zara shook the old man's hand and thanked him for the conversation. As she joined the immigration queue, she felt calmer and more confident than she did at the start of the journey.

Her father was waiting at the station exit, waving and smiling. Zara ran towards him, no longer thinking about the nervousness she felt hours before.

S12.title: The Best Hari Raya
S12.passage:
Eight-year-old Aiman looked forward to Hari Raya every year. This year, Grandma promised to teach him how to make ketupat — the diamond-shaped rice cakes wrapped in coconut leaves.

On the morning of Hari Raya, the whole family was busy. Father hung up the green lights along the corridor. Mother arranged the kuih on trays in the living room. Grandma sat in the kitchen, her nimble fingers weaving the coconut leaves into shape.

'Come, Aiman,' she called. Aiman sat beside her and watched every movement carefully. 'It looks easy, but you need patience,' Grandma said with a smile.

Aiman tried. His first attempt was too loose and the coconut leaves came apart. His second attempt was too tight. But on his third try, Grandma nodded. 'Better,' she said quietly.

By noon, they made over fifty pieces of ketupat. When the guests arrived, Aiman could not wait to tell them he helped make the ketupat himself. One uncle tasted a piece and said, 'This is the best ketupat I have ever eaten!'

Aiman beamed with pride. He knew the uncle was probably exaggerating, but it did not matter. It was the best Hari Raya he ever had.

S13.title: A Small Act
S13.passage:
Ten-year-old Reuben was walking to school on a rainy Tuesday when he spotted an old man sitting on the ground near the post office. The man's cane slipped out of his reach and he could not get up on his own.

Reuben stopped and looked around. Several adults walked past without stopping. Reuben hesitated for a moment — he was already running late for school.

Then he made his decision. He walked over, picked up the cane and handed it to the man. Then he gently held the man's arm and helped him to his feet.

'Thank you, young man,' the old man said breathlessly. 'My name is Mr Wong. I live just around the corner.'

Reuben walked Mr Wong home, even though it added ten minutes to his journey. When he finally arrived at school, his teacher noticed he was late. Reuben explained what happened.

The teacher said nothing for a moment. Then she smiled and said, 'The bell can wait. Some things are more important than being on time.'

S14.title: The Photography Club
S14.passage:
Every Thursday afternoon, the members of Riverside Primary's Photography Club met in Room 12 to review their work and learn new skills. The club had ten members and their teacher-in-charge was Mrs Yeo, a former professional photographer.

One Thursday, Mrs Yeo set them a challenge. 'Next week, I want each of you to bring one photograph that tells a story. No people — only nature.'

Twelve-year-old Ethan spent the whole weekend searching for the perfect shot. On Saturday morning, he noticed dew drops on a spider's web in his garden. He watched patiently as a bee landed in the centre of the web. At exactly the right moment, he pressed the button.

When he developed the photo, Ethan stared at it for a long time. The dew drops sparkled like tiny diamonds. The bee was perfectly in focus. The web stretched across the frame like a delicate net.

The following Thursday, Mrs Yeo looked at all the photos carefully. She held up Ethan's photo for the class to see. 'This one,' she said quietly, 'has a story and a soul.'

Ethan did not fully understand what she meant. But when he looked at the photo again later, he smiled. He did not just take a picture. He captured a moment.

S15.title: The Science Project
S15.passage:
It was the last week of term and Class 3C had to complete their science project on insects. Each group had to observe an insect for two weeks, record what they saw and present their findings to the class.

Ten-year-old Maya was in a group with her friends Deen and Siti. Their insect was the ant. Every day after school, the three of them crouched by the ant colony near the school drain and watched carefully.

One afternoon, Siti noticed that the ants were carrying tiny white eggs. 'The queen is moving her eggs to a safer place,' Maya said. She read about this in a library book. Deen quickly took notes while Maya pointed out each ant's role.

On presentation day, their group went last. Maya spoke clearly about the ant colony's structure. Deen explained the roles of the queen, the worker ants and the soldier ants. Siti showed the photographs she took during their observations.

When they finished, Mrs Chen, their science teacher, nodded slowly. 'You three clearly spent a lot of time observing,' she said. 'This is what real science looks like.'

Maya smiled. She started the project thinking insects were boring. She ended it thinking they were one of the most fascinating creatures on Earth.

S17.title: The Sleeping Cheetah
S17.passage:
Class 3B was on a school trip to the wildlife park. The students were excited, clutching their clipboards and worksheets. Their task was to observe one animal closely and write down three interesting facts about it.

Most students rushed to the lion enclosure or the elephant zone. But ten-year-old Faiz walked quietly to a smaller enclosure at the side. There, lying in the shade of a tall rock, was a cheetah.

The cheetah was asleep. Its spotted coat rose and fell with each slow breath. Faiz sat down on a bench and watched. He did not write anything yet. He just looked.

After ten minutes, the cheetah opened one eye. It looked directly at Faiz. Then it stretched, yawned and curled up again.

Faiz smiled and began to write. He wrote about the cheetah's spotted coat, its long tail that helped it balance when running, and the black lines on its face that looked like tear marks.

'You spent the whole time at one enclosure?' his friend asked after the trip.

'Yes,' said Faiz. 'And I learned more than anyone else today.'

S22.title: One Wrong Note
S22.passage:
Twelve-year-old Jamal practised the same piano piece for four months. It was a difficult piece, full of fast runs and sudden changes in volume, and he knew every note by heart. Tonight was the school concert, and he was the closing act.

When Jamal walked onto the stage, the lights were bright and the hall was packed. He sat at the grand piano, placed his hands on the keys and began.

The first half went perfectly. Then, in the third movement, his fingers slipped. He hit a wrong note — loud and clear in the quiet hall. He felt his face go red.

But Jamal did not stop. He steadied himself, took a breath and kept playing. The mistake faded behind him as the music carried on.

When the last note rang out, there was a moment of silence. Then the audience erupted. They rose to their feet and clapped. His music teacher, Mr Chua, was standing at the side of the stage with a wide smile.

'That was the bravest thing I have seen on this stage in twenty years,' Mr Chua said afterwards. 'Anyone can play a perfect piece. But only a true musician carries on after making a mistake.'

S23.title: The Best Playground
S23.passage:
For nine-year-old Hana, the old playground at the end of her block was the best place in the world. It had a rusty slide that squeaked, a single roundabout and two swings. Nothing about it was new or exciting. But it was where Hana learned to pump the swings on her own, where she made her best friend Siti on a rainy Wednesday afternoon, and where she always went when she felt sad or happy or simply restless.

One afternoon, Hana came home from school to find a notice pasted on the gate. The playground would be demolished the following week to make way for a new multi-purpose fitness area.

Hana felt a sudden tightness in her chest. She ran to the playground, sat on her favourite swing and pushed off slowly. The chain creaked. The sky was turning orange.

'Are you upset?' asked a voice. It was Siti, sitting on the other swing.

'It's just a playground,' Hana said. But her voice was quiet.

'I know,' said Siti. 'But it was our playground.'

The two of them swung in silence as the sun went down. When the streetlights came on, they finally walked home. Hana did not say anything, but she felt a little lighter.

The new fitness area opened three months later. It had bright equipment and a smooth path for jogging. Hana used it sometimes. But she never forgot the rusty swing that squeaked.

S26.title: A Week Without Sugar
S26.passage:
It started as a dare. During lunch on Monday, Kai bet his friend Omar that he could go an entire week without eating any sugar. Omar laughed. 'You won't last a day,' he said.

Tuesday was the hardest. Kai walked past the canteen snack corner without buying anything. He counted the gummy bears in his pencil case and put them back without eating a single one. By afternoon, he had a headache.

On Wednesday, Kai found that drinking water helped when he felt the urge for something sweet. He also ate an apple after lunch, which surprised him — he did not usually like apples much, but it tasted better than he remembered.

By Thursday, the headaches were gone. Kai noticed he felt more alert in class and did not fall asleep during afternoon lessons the way he sometimes did.

Friday arrived, and Kai succeeded. When he told Omar, Omar looked genuinely impressed. 'I honestly thought you would give up on day one,' he said.

Kai smiled. He did not say anything about the packet of sweets he had already bought for Saturday. But he also knew something had changed. He did not crave sugar the way he once did.

S27.title: The Broken Pot
S27.passage:
Class 3E arrived at the Heritage Museum on a Tuesday morning. Their teacher, Mr Loh, had one rule: look with your eyes, not your hands.

The first gallery was full of ancient pottery from South-East Asia. While the guide was explaining the history of a particular clay pot, a boy named Ivan leaned too close. He lost his balance, and his elbow caught the edge of a rope barrier. The barrier toppled, and the museum's smallest pot — a replica, thankfully — fell and shattered on the marble floor.

Everyone went very still. Ivan's face turned red. He looked at Mr Loh.

Mr Loh did not shout. He walked over to the museum attendant, spoke quietly and then came back. 'It was a replica,' he said calmly. 'No harm done. Now, what can everyone learn from this?'

A girl named Rina put her hand up. 'To respect the rules,' she said.

'Good,' said Mr Loh. 'And also — it is easier to break something than to make it.' He picked up one of the large shards and held it up. 'Look at this. A craftsman spent weeks shaping this pot. And it took one second to break.'

Ivan nodded slowly. He did not say anything for the rest of the museum visit. But when they reached the ancient weaving gallery at the end, he was the most careful one there.

S28.title: The Map in the Wall
S28.passage:
It was Priya who noticed it first. While she was leaning against the crumbling wall of the old shophouse, her hand felt something beneath the peeling paint — a raised edge, like the border of a frame. She looked closer. There, barely visible under decades of old white paint, was a map.

She called the others: her neighbour Reuben and her cousin Amara. Together, they spent the next forty minutes carefully brushing away loose paint with their fingers. Slowly, a hand-drawn map of the neighbourhood came into view — but the neighbourhood looked very different from how it did today.

There were pathways that no longer existed. Buildings that were now carparks. And at the centre of the map, circled in red ink, was a location that none of them recognised: 'The Keeper's Room'.

'This must be from decades ago,' Reuben said.

'We have to find out where this room is,' said Amara.

Preya photographed the map with her phone. She knew the local history group met every Saturday morning. She also knew her grandmother once lived in this neighbourhood since she was a child.

That Saturday, she brought the photograph as well as her grandmother.

S30.title: The Fisherman's Wish
S30.passage:
Long ago, a poor fisherman caught a golden fish in his net. The fish spoke in a clear, calm voice. 'Release me,' it said, 'and I will grant you one wish.'

The fisherman thought carefully. His family needed many things — a better boat, a larger house, enough food for winter. But instead, he made a simple request. 'I wish for my daughter to be healed,' he said, 'for she has been unwell for three years.'

The golden fish was quiet for a moment. Then it said, 'Your wish is granted.' The fish slipped back into the sea and disappeared.

When the fisherman returned home, his daughter was sitting up in bed, her cheeks pink and her eyes bright. She smiled when she saw him and said she felt better since noon.

The fisherman's neighbours were astonished. They asked him how he had managed it. He told them about the golden fish.

'You wasted the wish!' one neighbour said. 'You could have asked for gold, or a palace!'

The fisherman simply shook his head. He had no regrets.

Years later, when his daughter grew up to be a kind and generous woman, everyone in the village agreed that the fisherman made the wisest choice of all.

S31.title: The Notebook
S31.passage:
Twelve-year-old Farah found a black notebook on the seat of Bus 67 on a Wednesday afternoon. She nearly left it where it was — it was not hers, and she was already running late. But she picked it up.

The notebook had no name on the cover. Inside, she found page after page of pencil drawings — birds, trees, faces, and at the back, a half-finished sketch of a street that looked familiar. She turned to the first page. Underneath the first drawing was a small inscription: 'For whoever finds this — please keep it safe.'

Farah brought the notebook home and placed it on her desk. She looked at the drawings every evening that week. She thought about the person who made them — someone careful, someone patient, someone who looked at the world closely.

She decided she had to return it. She went back to the bus stop and spoke to the driver of Bus 67. He did not recognise the notebook but told her to check with the transport company's lost property office.

At the lost property office, a young man was already waiting. He looked up when Farah walked in, saw the notebook in her hands and stood up quickly.

'That's mine,' he said.

Farah handed it over. The young man held the notebook for a moment and exhaled slowly. 'I looked for this for two weeks,' he said. 'Thank you.'

On the bus home, Farah felt lighter than she had in a long time.

S32.title: The Message
S32.passage:
On a Tuesday afternoon, eleven-year-old Dani received a message on the class group chat. It said that the science test on Friday was cancelled. She felt a wave of relief — she had not started studying yet.

But something felt off. The message was sent by an account she did not recognise. She checked with her friend Lena, who had not seen any official notice from the teacher.

Dani decided to check with Mr Woo directly. She sent him a polite message asking whether the test was still on. His reply came within minutes: the test was very much on.

The next day at school, Dani told her classmates. Several of them had already stopped studying, believing the false message. They were upset — but also relieved that Dani found out in time.

Mr Woo addressed the class about the incident. 'This is exactly why we must check the source of every message before we believe it,' he said. 'A single unverified message caused five students to waste a study night.'

Dani felt grateful she trusted her instincts. She learned something that no classroom lesson could fully teach: the importance of questioning what you read.

S33.title: The Wall
S33.passage:
Class 3F arrived at the adventure camp on a Monday morning. Their first challenge was a six-metre climbing wall. From the ground, it looked enormous.

Most students cheered and lined up eagerly. But a boy named Wei stood at the back. His palms were sweating. He had never liked heights.

When it was his turn, Wei put on his harness and approached the wall. He placed his hands on the first holds. Then he stopped. His feet felt glued to the ground.

'Take one step,' said the instructor quietly.

Wei looked up. The wall seemed impossibly high. He looked down at the instructor. Then he looked up again and took one step.

And then another. And another.

He did not reach the top. He stopped about halfway up. But when he came down, his classmates — even those who had reached the top — clapped for him.

'Why are they clapping?' Wei asked the instructor. 'I didn't make it to the top.'

The instructor smiled. 'They're clapping because they saw what it took for you to get even halfway.'

S34.title: The Last Kopi Uncle
S34.passage:
Every morning at six, Uncle Beng opened the shutters of his coffee stall in Tanjong Pagar. He ran the stall for over forty years. The stall was not much to look at — four plastic chairs, two wooden tables, a blackboard menu and a battered aluminium kettle. But the coffee was famous.

People came from different parts of Singapore just to have a cup of Uncle Beng's kopi. Some were regulars who started coming when they were children. Others came after reading about the stall online.

One Tuesday morning, a journalist arrived. She was writing an article about the last of Singapore's traditional kopi stallholders.

'Do you worry the old ways will disappear?' she asked.

Uncle Beng poured coffee with a steady hand. 'Everything changes,' he said. 'But kopi — real kopi — will always find its people.'

He placed two cups on the counter. 'Have a seat,' he said.

The journalist drank her coffee slowly. It was unlike anything she had tasted in a modern café. It was strong and dark, with a sweetness that crept in at the end.

'Will you teach someone to take over?' she asked.

'My daughter is learning,' he said simply. 'She starts at five every morning.'

S35.title: The Long Note
S35.passage:
Twelve-year-old Clara studied the cello for three years. She was good — her teacher said so — but she could never quite believe it. Every time she made a mistake in class, she felt certain everyone was judging her.

The school's annual music recital was in three weeks. This year, Clara was asked to perform a solo. She had never performed alone in front of an audience before.

For the next three weeks, she practised every evening after dinner. She played the piece hundreds of times. She made mistakes, corrected them, and made them again. Slowly, the piece became part of her.

On the night of the recital, Clara sat in the wings backstage, listening to the other performers. Her hands were cold. When her name was called, she walked to the centre of the stage.

She closed her eyes, placed her bow on the strings and played the opening note. It was long and clear. Everything else — the audience, the lights, the cold hands — seemed to fall away.

When the last note ended, there was a pause. Then the hall filled with applause.

Afterwards, her teacher came backstage. 'You played every note,' she said. 'But what I heard tonight was more than the notes.'

S36.title: The Last Train
S36.passage:
It was eleven minutes past ten when eleven-year-old Sam looked up at the departure board and felt his stomach drop. The last train to Boon Lay departed three minutes ago. He was stranded at City Hall station with an empty EZ-Link card and his phone showing four percent battery.

Sam pressed himself against the wall near the exit, trying to think. He stayed too long at his cousin's birthday party and ignored the two messages his mother sent reminding him to leave early.

A station officer in a green vest noticed him and walked over. 'Are you alright, young man?' she asked.

Sam explained his situation. The officer's name tag read 'Chloe'. She did not scold him. Instead, she led him to the station control room and helped him call his mother using the station's phone.

His mother arrived forty minutes later. She was not angry — she looked more worried than upset. 'Next time, you read my messages,' she said quietly.

On the drive home, Sam stared out of the window. He thought about how a single choice — staying just a little longer — had led to this entire situation. He resolved never to miss the last train again.

S38.title: Saturday Mornings
S38.passage:
Every Saturday morning, without fail, nine-year-old Nora took the bus to her grandfather's flat in Toa Payoh. It was a fifteen-minute ride she made so many times that she could close her eyes and know exactly when to pull the bell.

Grandpa Lin was always at the door before she knocked. He had a habit of watching for the bus from his kitchen window, and the moment he spotted her yellow school bag through the glass, he would shuffle towards the door.

Their Saturday mornings followed a comfortable routine. Grandpa made kaya toast and soft-boiled eggs while Nora set the table. They ate slowly, and Grandpa told stories — about growing up in a kampung, about his first job at the docks, about the time he cycled from Toa Payoh to Changi just to impress a girl.

'Was that girl Grandma?' Nora always asked.

'Every time,' Grandpa always replied, with a smile that had not changed in forty years.

One Saturday, Nora arrived to find Grandpa asleep in his armchair. She let herself in quietly with the spare key and made the kaya toast herself. When Grandpa woke, he looked at the table and then at her, and something moved across his face that sat between a smile and sadness — something in between.

'You are more like your grandmother every day,' he said.

S40.title: The Last Leg
S40.passage:
The score between Red House and Blue House was tied at forty-eight points each going into the final event: the 4x100 metre relay. Whoever won this race would win the Sports Day championship.

Red House had the fastest individual sprinter in the school — a girl named Aisha. But the relay is not just about individual speed. The baton must be passed cleanly, and the team must run as one.

Blue House got off to a strong start. Their first two runners built a three-metre lead. By the third leg, the gap had widened to five metres.

Then Aisha stepped onto the track for the final leg. She ran not just with her legs but with everything she had. The crowd went quiet first — then erupted as she closed the gap metre by metre.

With twenty metres to go, she pulled level. With ten, she was ahead.

Red House crossed the finish line first by a fraction of a second.

In the changing room afterwards, Aisha sat quietly. Her teammates expected her to be celebrating. Instead, she said, 'I almost didn't catch up. We need to work on the third handover.'

That is what made her a leader.

S41.title: The Last Box
S41.passage:
The removal lorry pulled away at seven in the evening, leaving the family of four standing in a flat full of boxes. Ten-year-old Zara had not said a word since they arrived.

Her mother noticed. 'It will feel like home soon,' she said.

Zara said nothing. She went to what was now her bedroom and sat on the bare mattress. The walls were white. There were no drawings pinned to them, no shelves of books, no familiar shadows.

Her father appeared in the doorway with a box in his arms. It was labelled 'ZARA — IMPORTANT'. He placed it gently on the floor and left without speaking.

Zara opened it slowly. Inside were her drawing pads, her coloured pencils, her stack of library books and — at the very bottom — a small framed photograph of her and her best friend Chloe, taken at the school garden on the last day of term.

She picked up a pencil and began drawing. First the outline of the window. Then the tree she could see outside. Then, slowly, the room itself.

By nine o'clock, there were three drawings pinned to the white wall.

When her mother came to say goodnight, Zara looked up and said, 'I think I can make this work.'

S42.title: How People Learn New Skills
S42.passage:
Learning a new skill is one of the most rewarding experiences a person can have, but it rarely follows a straight line. Research shows that skill development typically happens in three stages.

In the first stage, everything feels clumsy and slow. A beginner has to think about every step — where to place their fingers, how to hold a tool, when to apply pressure. This conscious effort is tiring and mistakes are frequent.

In the second stage, some actions start to feel more natural. The learner no longer has to think about every small movement. This is when practice becomes most valuable, because the brain is beginning to form reliable pathways for the new skill.

In the third stage, the skill feels automatic. An expert pianist does not think about individual notes — they feel the music. A skilled chef does not measure every ingredient — they sense when something is right. At this stage, the learner has moved from thinking to feeling.

What makes the difference between those who reach stage three and those who stop at stage one? Research points to one factor above all others: the willingness to tolerate the discomfort of being a beginner.

S43.title: The River's Secret
S43.passage:
The sign at the entrance to the freshwater zone read: 'Seven percent of all known animal species live in freshwater. Yet freshwater makes up less than one percent of the Earth's habitable surface.'

Twelve-year-old Theo read the sign twice. He had always thought of rivers as ordinary. He grew up next to the Kallang River and never thought much about what lived beneath its surface.

Inside the exhibit, he pressed his face against the glass of the largest tank. A fat, slow-moving arapaima drifted past — one of the largest freshwater fish in the world, over two metres long. Beside it, a school of silver dollar fish caught the light and flashed like coins.

A keeper in a green vest appeared. 'Do you know how they breathe?' she asked Theo, nodding at the arapaima.

Theo shook his head.

'They can breathe air,' she said. 'Their swim bladder works like a lung. During dry season when rivers shrink and oxygen levels drop, they swim to the surface and gulp air.'

Theo stared. 'So they survive conditions that would kill most fish?'

'Exactly,' said the keeper. 'They've been doing it for two hundred million years.'

Theo looked at the arapaima again. It was not beautiful in the way that coral reef fish were beautiful. But there was something about it — something ancient and unstoppable — that he found more impressive.

S44.title: The Bread That Waited
S44.passage:
Thirteen-year-old Dev watched his grandmother bake bread for as long as he could remember. Her hands moved without measuring — a pinch of this, a handful of that. Dev had always wondered if he could do the same.

One Saturday morning, he decided to try. He found the recipe card in the back of the recipe book — her handwriting, faded but legible. He followed every step. He measured. He kneaded for eight minutes by the clock. He let the dough rise for an hour.

The result was dense and flat. Nothing like his grandmother's bread.

He said nothing at dinner. But his grandmother noticed. After the dishes were cleared, she came and sat across from him.

'You tried the bread,' she said. It was not a question.

Dev nodded. 'It was wrong,' he said. 'The recipe is the same but mine didn't come out like yours.'

His grandmother smiled. 'The recipe is the same. But you cannot bake it the way I do yet. I've made that bread four hundred times. Every time teaches you something the recipe doesn't say.'

Dev looked at his hands. 'So I just have to keep making it?' he asked.

'Yes,' she said. 'And one day your bread will taste different from mine. Not worse. Just yours.'

S45.title: The Open House
S45.passage:
Every year on the first day of Hari Raya, Mdm Aisha opened her door to everyone on the floor — regardless of race or religion. She was doing this.

This year, her new neighbour, a forty-year-old man named Mr Tan, hesitated at the entrance. He moved in only three weeks before and felt unsure about intruding on a family occasion.

'Come in, come in,' said Mdm Aisha, waving him forward. 'There is more than enough.'

Mr Tan removed his shoes and stepped inside. On the table were dishes he had never tasted before — rendang, lemang and pineapple tarts. Mdm Aisha's daughter, Rina, handed him a plate and showed him what each dish was.

By the end of the afternoon, Mr Tan had laughed more than he had in months. As he stood to leave, he turned to Mdm Aisha and said, 'I did not expect to feel so at home.'

Mdm Aisha smiled. 'That is what an open house is for,' she said.

At the end of the afternoon, Mr Tan lingered by the door. The table was cleared, but the warmth in the room remained. He thought about how long he had hesitated at the entrance. Next year, he told himself, he would bring something — perhaps a tin of cookies, or some mooncakes for a different celebration. He was not sure of the customs yet. But he was learning.

S47.title: The Empty Seat
S47.passage:
On the first day of school after the June holidays, twelve-year-old Anya sat down and noticed that the seat next to her was empty. Her best friend Jess moved to Australia.

The teacher introduced a new student. Her name was Clara, and she stood at the front with her eyes fixed on her shoes. Anya remembered her own first day at this school — how long the classroom had seemed, and how nobody had spoken to her for the entire morning.

She moved her bag off the chair beside her.

'You can sit here,' she said.

Clara looked up. She hesitated, then walked over and sat down.

They did not speak much for the first week. But Anya made sure to save the seat every day. On Friday, Clara brought two rice crispy treats wrapped in foil. She placed one quietly on Anya's desk.

Anya looked at the treat, then at Clara.

'Thank you,' she said.

Clara smiled — the first real smile Anya saw from her all week. 'Thank you for the seat,' Clara said.

By the end of the second week, they had discovered they both liked the same author. Anya lent Clara three books in a single afternoon. Clara returned them all the following Monday with tiny sticky notes inside marking her favourite lines. Neither of them mentioned the empty seat or the rice crispy treat again. They did not need to.

S48.title: How to Stay Safe During a Thunderstorm
S48.passage:
Singapore experiences thunderstorms more than 170 days a year, making it one of the world's most storm-prone countries. Understanding what happens during a thunderstorm and how to stay safe can make a real difference.

A thunderstorm forms when warm, moist air rises rapidly and meets cooler air high in the atmosphere. This creates large storm clouds that produce lightning and thunder. Lightning is a powerful electrical discharge, and the thunder we hear is the sound it makes as it heats the air around it. Because light travels faster than sound, we always see lightning before we hear thunder. Counting the seconds between the flash and the bang tells you how far away the storm is — roughly one kilometre for every three seconds.

During a thunderstorm, there are several safety rules to follow. You should stay indoors and away from windows. Avoid using electrical appliances and unplug devices where possible. If you are outdoors, do not shelter under a tree, as trees attract lightning. Move to a low-lying area instead and crouch down with your feet together and your hands over your ears.

Thunderstorms in Singapore usually pass within thirty to sixty minutes. After the rain stops, it is important to check for flooded paths and fallen branches before going outside.

S49.title: Sixty Seconds
S49.passage:
The alarm sounded at 2.47 in the afternoon. By 2.48, Senior Station Inspector Ravi had already led his team out of the station.

The call was for a kitchen fire in a third-floor flat on Clementi Avenue. When the engine arrived, smoke was pouring from an open window. Ravi's team pulled on their breathing masks and went in.

The fire was small — a forgotten pan on the stove. They put it out in under two minutes. But in the corridor outside, they found an elderly man who could not walk. He was trying to reach the staircase when the smoke overcame him.

Ravi lifted the man onto his back and carried him down three flights of stairs without stopping.

The paramedics were waiting outside. The man, who was seventy-eight years old, was taken to hospital and later confirmed to be in stable condition.

At the debrief that evening, Ravi reminded his team: 'The fire was the easy part. It is always the person who needs the most time.'

Ravi did not speak on the way back to the station. At the debrief, he set his helmet on the table and looked at his team. Each of them knew what the other was thinking: the man in the corridor could have been anyone's grandfather. That thought did not make the work harder. It made it more important.

S50.title: The Last Spin
S50.passage:
It was the final round of the gasing competition, and nine-year-old Arif had one chance left.

All morning, he watched the older boys launch their tops with a single, practiced flick of the wrist. Their tops spun for minutes at a time, gliding slowly across the smooth concrete pad. Arif's best spin so far had lasted forty-three seconds.

His grandfather, who had taught him everything he knew about gasing, sat in the third row of the plastic chairs. He did not wave or call out. He simply watched.

Arif stepped to the line. He wound the rope around the top slowly, the way his grandfather had shown him — tight, even, patient.

He threw.

The top landed perfectly and spun without wobbling. Arif did not watch it. He watched his grandfather's face instead.

At sixty seconds, the crowd began to count. At seventy, some stood up. At eighty-three seconds, the judge raised the green flag.

Arif looked at his grandfather. The old man pressed his lips together and nodded once — the same nod he gave when something was done correctly.

That was enough.

Outside, the other competitors had already left. Arif stayed a little longer, watching the empty concrete pad where the tops had spun. He wanted to remember exactly how the rope felt in his hands.

S52.title: Two Mornings
S52.passage:
Eleven-year-old Priya grew up in a flat in Ang Mo Kio. She never visited a farm before.

On the first morning, she woke at five to help her aunt milk the cows. It was still dark. Everything smelled of earth and animals. She held the bucket so tightly her knuckles went white.

Her aunt did not explain. She simply showed her — slow, even strokes, the same rhythm again and again. Priya tried. The cow shifted, and she spilled half the bucket.

'Again,' said her aunt. There was no irritation in her voice. Just the word.

On the second morning, Priya woke at four-thirty — half an hour early. She was already in the barn when her aunt arrived.

'You came back,' said her aunt.

'I spilled,' said Priya.

Her aunt handed her the bucket. 'That is why you came back.'

By seven o'clock, the milk was done and the cows were calm. Priya's arms ached, but she did not mention it.

On the bus home, Priya sat without speaking. Her arms still ached. She looked at her hands and thought about the rhythm her aunt had shown her — slow, even, patient. She realised she could still feel the motion, like a small muscle memory she had not owned before that morning.

S53.title: The Book in the Corner
S53.passage:
The book was always in the same corner. Every Saturday, nine-year-old Jonas walked past the other shelves — the adventure books, the science books, the graphic novels — and went straight to that corner.

The book was too difficult for him. He knew that. The words were long and the sentences ran over two lines. But he liked the cover: a boy standing at the edge of a cliff, looking out at a sea of clouds.

He never borrowed it. He just sat down and tried to read it. Sometimes he got through one page. Once, on a day when the library was particularly quiet, he got through three.

One Saturday, the corner was empty. The book was gone.

Jonas stood and stared at the gap in the shelf for a long time. Then he went to the librarian.

'Someone borrowed the book in the corner,' he said. 'The one with the boy on the cliff.'

The librarian checked the screen. 'It will be back in three weeks,' she said.

Jonas nodded. 'I'll be here,' he said.

He sat down in the corner with a different book. But he did not read it. He thought about the boy on the cliff and the sea of clouds below.

S55.title: The Pangolin and the Girl
S55.passage:
Ten-year-old Mei had never seen a pangolin before. She was cycling home from school when she spotted the creature by the drain — curled into a ball, completely still.

She knew enough not to touch it. Instead, she took a photograph with her mother's phone and called the wildlife rescue number on a poster at the library.

The officer who answered was calm and asked her clear questions: Where exactly was she? Was the animal breathing? Was there any blood? Mei answered each one carefully, keeping her eyes on the pangolin.

Thirty minutes later, a rescue van arrived. The officer — a tall woman named Dr Farah — crouched down beside the pangolin. 'It's dehydrated and frightened,' she said, 'but it will be fine.'

She lifted the pangolin gently into a ventilated box lined with dry leaves, then turned to Mei.

'You did exactly the right thing,' she said. 'Most people either run away or try to pick it up. You stayed calm and called for help.'

Mei watched the van drive away. She thought about the pangolin — one of the world's most trafficked animals — and decided, right there on the pavement, that she wanted to work with animals one day.

S56.title: Window Seat
S56.passage:
Eight-year-old Zara never flew on a plane before this trip. She expected it to be loud, and it was. But it was also — unexpectedly — beautiful.

From her window seat, she watched the ground disappear. Singapore shrank below her: highways became threads, buildings became squares, and the sea turned into a flat silver mirror. Then the clouds rose up around the plane, and she could no longer see the ground at all.

She pressed her nose against the cold glass and stared.

Her father, who was sitting in the middle seat reading a magazine, glanced up. 'You all right?'

'Dad,' said Zara quietly, 'is this what the world looks like from up here all the time?'

Her father smiled. 'Every time,' he said.

Zara turned back to the window. Below her, the clouds formed a white landscape. Hills of cloud. Plains of cloud. A whole other world above the one she knew from the ground.

She did not touch her in-flight meal. She did not use the entertainment screen. She sat with her face turned to the window for the entire four-hour flight, watching the light change across the clouds as the sun moved slowly west.

S57.title: Why Do Ice Cubes Melt Faster in Salt Water?
S57.passage:
Have you ever noticed that roads are sprinkled with salt during winter in cold countries? The reason is connected to a simple scientific principle: salt lowers the freezing point of water.

Pure water freezes at zero degrees Celsius. When salt is added to water, the water molecules become harder to freeze, so the freezing point drops below zero. This means that a saltwater solution stays liquid at temperatures where pure water would already be solid ice.

This same principle explains why ice cubes melt faster in salt water than in plain water. When you drop an ice cube into a glass of salt water, the salt water immediately begins pulling heat from the ice. The more salt there is in the water, the lower the freezing point drops, and the faster the ice melts.

You can test this yourself. Fill two identical glasses — one with plain water and one with salt water — and add a same-sized ice cube to each. Observe what happens over five minutes and record the results.

This kind of experiment is called a controlled experiment. You change only one variable — the salt — and keep everything else the same: the amount of water, the size of the ice cube, the room temperature. This way, you can be sure that any difference in the results is caused by the salt alone.

S58.title: Saturday at the Market
S58.passage:
Every Saturday, nine-year-old Wei woke early and followed his grandfather to the wet market at Tekka. It was their ritual — just the two of them, before the rest of the family stirred.

His grandfather moved through the stalls like water, pausing here, nodding there, tasting a sliver of something before deciding. Wei knew enough to be patient. The market was not a place to rush.

At the fish stall, Uncle Raju always saved the best threadfin for their family. 'For you, Mr Lim — still swimming when it arrived this morning,' he would say, and grandfather would inspect it closely, turn it once, then nod.

Wei did not eat fish. But he liked the ceremony of it.

At the tofu stall, the auntie sliced quickly and silently — cubes of white, firm and soft, stacked in a green basin. She never needed to be told how much. She knew.

On the way home, grandfather carried the bags. Wei always asked to carry one, and grandfather always let him — the lightest one. Neither mentioned this.

At home, grandmother would begin to cook while grandfather washed the vegetables over the sink. Wei sat at the kitchen table, and the smell of garlic and old wood filled the flat.

S59.title: The Message
S59.passage:
It started with one message.

Nina received it on the class chat group on a Monday morning: a photo of her, taken at Sports Day, with a caption that made fun of the way she ran. She did not know who sent it — the account used a fake name she did not recognise.

By lunchtime, twelve people laughed at it.

Nina did not go to the canteen that day. She sat at her desk and stared at her pencil case.

Her form teacher, Mrs Tan, noticed. At the end of the day, she asked Nina to stay behind.

'I didn't want to make a fuss,' Nina said.

Mrs Tan sat down across from her. 'Making a fuss,' she said quietly, 'is exactly what we need to do when something like this happens. Not to punish. To fix.'

Nina showed her the screenshot. Mrs Tan took her time looking at it, then nodded.

'This is not a joke,' she said. 'It is not harmless. And it is not going to continue.'

By the next morning, the post was removed and the fake account was reported. Nina did not know what the school said to the students involved. But the laughing stopped.

S60.title: The Last Lesson
S60.passage:
On the last afternoon of Primary Three, Mrs Chen did something she never did before.

She handed out a strip of paper to every student and told them to write one sentence: what they wanted to be in twenty years.

The room went quiet. Students bent over their papers. Some wrote quickly, as if they always knew. Others stared at the ceiling, tapping their pencils.

Mrs Chen collected the strips without reading them. She sealed them inside a small envelope and taped it to the back of the classroom door.

'I will give this back to you when you finish Primary Six,' she said. 'By then, some of you will have changed your minds. Some of you will have found something new. And a few of you — maybe one or two — will be doing exactly what you wrote today.'

She smiled. 'But all of you — every single one — will be further along than you are now. That is the only thing I can promise you.'

Ahmed kept looking at the envelope after Mrs Chen turned back to the board. He wrote three words: 'help sick people.' He did not know what that would look like yet. But he meant every word.

S08.title: The Lost Wallet
S08.passage:
Nine-year-old Marcus was helping his mother carry the groceries when he saw a brown wallet on the floor near the checkout counter. He looked inside and found some cash and a name card that read: 'Mr David Tan, Block 44, Maple Avenue.'

'Mum, someone dropped this,' Marcus said, holding up the wallet. His mother smiled. 'What do you think you should do?' she asked.

Marcus thought carefully. He could keep the money — there was quite a lot inside. But he knew that was wrong. He handed the wallet to the customer service counter and told the officer what he found.

The officer took down Marcus's name and phone number. That evening, Mr Tan called their home. He sounded very relieved. He told Marcus's mother that the wallet contained money for his daughter's school trip, which was the very next day.

'Your son is a very honest boy,' Mr Tan said. He visited the next day and brought a box of biscuits as a thank-you gift. Marcus felt happier about returning the wallet than he would have felt keeping the money.

Nine-year-old Preethi could never make up her mind about what she wanted to be when she grew up. One week she wanted to be a scientist, the next a pilot, and the week after that, a baker.

One afternoon, her school organised a Career Day. Parents came in to talk about their jobs. The first speaker was Mr Hassan, a police officer. He told the students about the importance of keeping the community safe and working as a team.

The second speaker was Dr Lim, a children's doctor. She said the best part of her job was seeing a sick child recover and go home healthy. 'Nothing makes me happier,' she said with a warm smile.

The last speaker was Mrs Gomez, a school librarian. She spoke softly about how books could take a person anywhere in the world. 'Every book I shelve is a door to a new adventure,' she said.

After Career Day, Preethi sat quietly in the garden at home. She thought about all three speakers. Each of them loved what they did. Each of them helped people in a different way.

Preethi picked up the book she was reading and smiled. She still did not know what she wanted to be. But she knew one thing for certain — the best job was the one that made you feel proud every single day.

S18.title: A Dog Named Scout
S18.passage:
When Aiden was six years old, his parents brought home a small brown puppy. Aiden named him Scout. From the first day, the two were inseparable. Scout slept at the foot of Aiden's bed and waited by the door every afternoon for him to come home from school.

As Scout grew older, Aiden took on more responsibility. He learned to measure Scout's food carefully, brush his coat every evening and take him for walks even when it was raining. His mother watched quietly and smiled. Her shy, quiet boy was growing more confident every day.

One morning in Aiden's third year of primary school, Scout fell ill. He refused to eat and lay still in his basket with dull, half-closed eyes. Aiden was frightened. He sat beside Scout and stroked his fur gently, whispering, 'You'll be okay.'

At the vet's clinic, the doctor examined Scout and said he had a stomach infection. 'He will need medicine twice a day for five days,' she said.

Aiden gave Scout his medicine every morning and evening without missing a single dose. By the fifth day, Scout was wagging his tail again.

That evening, Aiden hugged Scout tightly. He realised that caring for a pet was not just about the fun parts. It was about being there — even on the hard days.

S19.title: The Right Thing to Do
S19.passage:
It was a bright Tuesday afternoon when eight-year-old Nora noticed something that made her stop in her tracks. An elderly man was trying to cross a busy road, but he looked confused and kept stepping forward and pulling back each time a car went by.

Nora hesitated. She was already late for her piano lesson, and her mother was waiting for her at the community centre just two blocks away. But the sight of the old man struggling made her feel uneasy.

She walked up to him. 'Excuse me, sir. Would you like me to help you cross?' she asked politely.

The old man looked at her with grateful eyes. 'Thank you, child. My eyesight is not very good these days.'

Nora held his arm gently and looked both ways carefully before guiding him across at the pedestrian crossing. On the other side, the old man thanked her warmly and went on his way.

When Nora arrived at the community centre, she explained to her mother what happened. Her mother did not say a single word about the lateness. Instead, she pulled Nora close and said quietly, 'I am very proud of you.'

S20.title: Stars in Her Eyes
S20.passage:
Eleven-year-old Priya wanted to be an astronaut from the age of four. Her bedroom ceiling was covered with glow-in-the-dark stars, and her bookshelf held more books about space than about anything else.

One evening, her school organised a visit to the Science Centre for a special planetarium show. Priya arrived thirty minutes early, claiming a seat in the very front row. While the other students chatted and played on their phones, Priya sat perfectly still, staring up at the dark dome above her.

When the show began, the dome lit up with thousands of simulated stars. The narrator explained how stars are born inside giant clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. Priya leaned forward in her seat, her notebook open on her lap. She wrote down every fact, every name and every number.

Afterward, a scientist named Dr Ariff stayed to answer questions. One by one, the other students gave short answers and walked away. But Priya stayed. She asked about the temperature at the core of a star, how long it takes light to travel from the nearest star to Earth and whether any current missions were searching for planets like ours.

Dr Ariff looked at her with a wide smile. 'You know,' he said, 'I have been visiting schools for fifteen years. I have never met a student quite like you.'

Priya did not know what to say. She just looked back up at the dome, which was now dark and still. She smiled quietly to herself.

S21.title: The Blank Canvas
S21.passage:
Every Thursday after school, twelve-year-old Omar went to the community art room. He went every Thursday for six months, but he never finished a single painting. He would start boldly — choosing the brightest colours, sweeping the brush across the canvas in long strokes — and then, halfway through, he would stop. Something always felt wrong.

'It doesn't look right,' he would mutter, and leave the half-finished canvas on the shelf.

The art teacher, Mrs Yip, noticed. One day, she placed a fresh canvas in front of Omar and sat down beside him.

'Why do you always stop?' she asked.

'Because it never looks the way I imagine it,' he said quietly.

Mrs Yip nodded slowly. 'That feeling,' she said, 'means you have a real eye for art. The gap between what you imagine and what you can do is exactly where improvement lives.'

Omar looked at the blank canvas. 'So I should keep going even when it looks wrong?'

'Especially then,' said Mrs Yip.

That afternoon, Omar started a painting of the view from the art room window. He painted past the point where he usually stopped. The result was not perfect. But for the first time, he had a finished painting — and it was his.

He looked at it for a long time. Then he picked up his brush and started another one.

S24.title: The Seahorse
S24.passage:
Of all the creatures in the ocean, the seahorse is one of the most unusual. It does not look like a typical fish. It has a horse-like head, a long curved neck and a body covered in bony rings instead of scales. Its eyes move independently of each other, which means it can look in two different directions at the same time.

Seahorses are very slow swimmers. They move upright through the water by fluttering their tiny dorsal fin very fast — up to fifty times per second. They use their curling tails to grip onto seagrass and coral so that strong currents do not sweep them away.

One of the most surprising facts about seahorses is that it is the male — not the female — that carries and gives birth to the young. The female deposits her eggs into a special pouch on the male's body. The male carries the eggs for several weeks until the baby seahorses are ready to swim out on their own.

Seahorses are also skilled hunters. They creep up slowly behind tiny shrimps and then snap them up with their long tube-like mouths so fast that the shrimp barely has time to react.

Sadly, seahorses are under threat. They are caught in fishing nets, collected for use in traditional medicine and lose their homes when seagrass meadows and coral reefs are destroyed. Conservation groups are working hard to protect them and restore the habitats they depend on.

S25.title: The Girl Who Fixed Things
S25.passage:
Nobody in the neighbourhood threw anything away without asking Nadia first. Toasters, fans, radios — if it was broken, they brought it to her. Nadia was eleven years old and her workshop was the corner of her bedroom, but she could fix almost anything with a screwdriver and a lot of patience.

One afternoon, her grandmother brought in an old clock that had stopped working. 'My father gave me this when I was young,' Grandma said. 'I thought it was lost forever.'

Nadia opened the back of the clock and peered inside. The spring was broken. She spent two hours bending and adjusting a replacement spring she made from a piece of wire. When she wound the clock up and placed it on the table, it began to tick again — slowly at first, then with a steady rhythm.

Grandma held the clock with two hands and was quiet for a long time. 'How do you know how to do all this?' she asked.

'I take things apart,' Nadia said simply. 'And then I figure out how to put them back together.'

That evening, Nadia sat in her corner and thought about what she wanted to do when she grew up. She did not think about fame or money. She thought about the sound of a clock ticking again. She thought about her grandmother's face.

S29.title: The Rooftop Garden
S29.passage:
When the principal of Greenfield Primary announced that an unused rooftop would be turned into a garden, the students were curious but unconvinced. 'What is the point of growing vegetables at school?' one student asked.

By the end of the year, those same students could not imagine school without it.

The project began in January with the students digging compost into large planters and sowing seeds of spinach, chilli and cherry tomatoes. At first, progress was slow and some seeds did not sprout at all. But by March, the rooftop had green shoots pushing upward from every planter.

The garden changed the way many students thought about food. Before the project, several admitted they had never thought about where vegetables came from. After growing them, they paid more attention to what they ate and wasted far less food at lunch.

The garden also brought students together. Children from different classes worked side by side during gardening sessions, learning each other's names. A boy named Darren, who had previously kept to himself, became one of the most active gardeners. By the end of the year, he made three close friends through the garden.

In December, the students organised a small harvest festival. They cooked a simple vegetable soup using everything they grew, and invited parents and teachers to join them.

S37.title: The Brave Chair
S37.passage:
Nine-year-old Priya had not been to the dentist in two years. Every time her mother suggested a visit, Priya found a reason to postpone it — a school project, a family outing, a stomach ache that appeared just in time.

But one Tuesday morning, Priya woke up with a sharp pain in her lower left molar. It throbbed steadily, like a tiny hammer tapping from the inside. She tried to ignore it, but by lunchtime, she could not chew her food properly.

Her mother made an appointment for that same afternoon. The clinic was small and brightly lit. Dr Nair, a tall woman with a gentle voice, welcomed Priya without any fuss. She examined the tooth quickly and explained that there was a cavity that needed to be filled.

'Will it hurt?' Priya asked.

'There will be a small pinch,' said Dr Nair. 'After that, you will feel nothing.'

She was right. The injection stung for two seconds. Then the whole left side of Priya's mouth felt like a thick cushion. The filling itself took twelve minutes.

Walking out, Priya felt something she had not expected: relief. Not just because it was over, but because it was so much smaller than the fear she carried for two years.

'You should have come sooner,' her mother said.

Priya nodded. She already knew.

S46.title: The Sandcastle Competition
S46.passage:
It was the last Saturday of the June holidays. The Sentosa Beach Festival had organised a sandcastle competition, and eight-year-old Kai planned his design for two weeks.

His plan was ambitious — a four-towered castle with a moat, a drawbridge made of driftwood and tiny flags made from paper clips and scraps of cloth. He had even drawn a blueprint on a piece of paper, which he kept folded in his pocket.

When the starting whistle blew, Kai's older sister Priya dug the foundations while Kai shaped the towers. They worked without stopping for an hour and a half.

With fifteen minutes left, disaster struck. A large wave slid up the beach and collapsed one entire wall of the castle.

Kai stared at the damage. Then, without a word, he began rebuilding.

They did not win first prize. A twelve-year-old boy named Sam built a replica of the Merlion that was judged the most creative entry. But Kai's castle won the special prize for Most Improved — because the judges watched him rebuild the fallen wall without complaint.

As the sky turned orange over the cable car station, Kai's father took a photograph of the battered castle standing proud in the late light. It was lopsided, shorter than planned and missing one tower entirely. But in the photograph, it looked exactly right.

S51.title: The Insect Architects
S51.passage:
Most people know that bees make honey. But the engineering inside a beehive is just as remarkable as the honey itself.

Bees build their hives from wax, which they produce inside their own bodies. A single worker bee produces only about one gram of wax in its entire lifetime. Yet a large hive may contain over one hundred thousand individual wax cells, all built to exactly the same six-sided shape.

The six-sided shape, called a hexagon, is not chosen by accident. It is the most efficient shape that exists: it uses the least amount of wax to create the most amount of storage space. Engineers and architects have studied the hexagon for centuries because of this property.

Inside each cell, bees store honey, pollen or eggs. The temperature inside the hive is kept at exactly thirty-five degrees Celsius at all times — warm enough for eggs to develop, cool enough to preserve the honey.

When a hive becomes too crowded, the queen bee leaves with half the colony to build a new home. The remaining bees raise a new queen. In this way, the colony survives and grows, generation after generation.

S39.title: The Last Card
S39.passage:
The school hall was full. Three hundred students sat in rows, facing a small stage lit by a single spotlight. On the stage stood a man in a black suit. He introduced himself as Marco.

Marco performed seven tricks that evening. He made a coin pass through a solid table. He caused a handkerchief to change colour three times in a row. He invited a girl named Priya to choose any card from a deck, memorise it and return it to the pack — then he produced it from inside a sealed envelope that sat on a chair since the show began.

But the final trick was the one everyone remembered.

Marco asked the audience to think of any number between one and ten. He did not ask anyone to say it out loud. Then he turned his back to the audience and said, 'The number most of you are thinking of is seven.'

A roar went up from the hall.

Later, a boy named Ethan asked his teacher how the trick worked. 'When people are asked for a number between one and ten,' his teacher said, 'most people choose seven. It's simply how the human brain tends to work.'

Ethan was quiet for a moment. 'So it wasn't really magic at all,' he said.

'Perhaps not,' said the teacher. 'But it felt like it, didn't it?'

S54.title: The Night Shift
S54.passage:
Marcus worked as a cleaner at Changi Airport for eleven years. He worked the night shift — from ten at night until six in the morning — when the terminals were quieter and the floors could be cleaned properly.

Most passengers did not notice him. They were tired, or rushing, or looking at their phones. A woman once walked straight through his wet-mopped section without pausing, leaving footprints across the section he had just finished.

Marcus did not say anything. He mopped it again.

There was a boy, perhaps nine or ten, who watched him one night from a seat near Gate C12. The boy's family was waiting for a late flight. He watched Marcus work for almost twenty minutes.

Then the boy walked over.

'Why do you clean at night?' he asked.

Marcus stopped and thought about it. 'Because when the sun comes up,' he said, 'I want everything to be ready.'

The boy looked around at the gleaming floor. 'I never thought about who cleans,' he said.

Marcus smiled. 'Not many people do,' he said. 'But someone has to.'

Marcus picked up his mop and cart and moved on to Gate C13. There were still four more sections to finish before six.
